title: Domes
hook: the dome as the heavens, with Christ Pantocrator looking down

segments.voice: Yesterday, the plain meeting house: white walls, clear glass, and a room kept bare on purpose. Your line was nothing between. What did you clear away yesterday, and what did the space feel like after? Day one thousand three hundred fifty-five.

Over the center of some Orthodox churches, the ceiling doesn't stop. It curves up and closes into a dome, and from its very top a face looks down. Christ, painted large. One hand raised in blessing. The other holding a book. Around him, in some churches, angels circle; lower down, prophets and apostles; lower still, the walls with their saints; and at the bottom, the people, standing, heads tipped back. Stand right under the center and the whole building seems to turn around that one face, the way a sky seems to turn around wherever you happen to be standing. Today: domes.

A dome is a round roof. In an Orthodox church, it's also a picture of the sky. Start there. Isaiah describes God as the one "that stretcheth out the heavens as a curtain, and spreadeth them out as a tent to dwell in." A tent over the whole earth. A dome builds that tent over one congregation: a curved heaven, with everyone underneath it at once. Then, what the sky says. "The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork." The psalm hears the real sky talking. A painted dome makes the talking easier to hear: instead of clouds, it shows faces, and the highest one is Christ. That image has a name: Christ Pantocrator. Pantocrator is a Greek word, and it appears in the New Testament itself. In the book of Revelation, the Lord says: "I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the ending, saith the Lord, which is, and which was, and which is to come, the Almighty." The Almighty, in the Greek, is pantokrator. So the face at the top of the dome is the one Revelation calls the beginning and the end. He blesses with one hand, and holds the gospel book with the other. Last, the order of the whole room. Heaven at the top, earth at the bottom, and the walls between them full of people who have lived on both. Orthodox Christians speak of the liturgy as heaven and earth worshiping together. Under a dome, the Lord's Prayer can be heard almost as a description of the room: "Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven." In that picture, heaven isn't far off up there. It's overhead.
screen: `THE HEAVENS DECLARE THE GLORY OF GOD.`
`IN EARTH, AS IT IS IN HEAVEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look up at a ceiling. Any ceiling. If you're outside, the sky. Settle, and breathe, and tip your head back gently. Let your eyes find the center point above you, and rest there. Then think of everyone else under that same roof, or that same sky, right now. If you pray, you can say the line from the psalm: the heavens declare the glory of God. Or simply stay under it, breathing, with heaven, or ceiling, or sky, overhead. The bell holds the time.
screen: `THE HEAVENS DECLARE THE GLORY OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Domes. In an Orthodox church, a round roof painted as the heavens, with Christ Pantocrator, the Almighty, looking down over everyone at once.
Your line: heaven overhead. Today, when you're in a room with other people, glance up once and notice that one ceiling covers all of you. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: In Orthodox churches built with a central dome, the dome is painted as the heavens, in some with Christ Pantocrator at its height, and worshipers stand beneath it during the Divine Liturgy.

myth: Pantocrator is a word that appears in the New Testament
in Revelation 1:8 the Greek pantokrator is rendered "the Almighty" in the King James.
an Orthodox dome is painted only to decorate the roof
it's a picture of the heavens, with Christ at the top and the people beneath.

fork.setup: you're painting the inside of a new dome. at its very top goes one image, seen from everywhere in the church. what goes there?
options: a starry sky with nothing in it
Christ, one hand blessing, the other holding a book
the names of everyone who built the church
fork.reveal: in Orthodox churches the height of the dome is a place for Christ Pantocrator, the one Revelation calls the Almighty.

original.note: Greek: the word the King James renders "the Almighty" in Revelation 1:8.

trapdoor: what you thought: a dome is just a round roof.
what it means: in an Orthodox church, a ceiling painted as the heavens, with Christ looking down.
what a scholar hears: the image's name, Pantocrator, is Revelation's own word for the Almighty.

notes: Greek of Revelation 1:8 has pantokrator for 'the Almighty'; confirm. No further etymology is claimed.

Descriptions of the Pantocrator image (hand raised in blessing, holding a book) and the descending order of angels, prophets, apostles and saints are general; an Orthodox Keeper should confirm, and confirm 'in some churches' is fair.
'Orthodox Christians speak of the liturgy as heaven and earth worshiping together': confirm this is a fair description of Orthodox teaching.
Pronunciation 'pan-doh-KRAH-tor' follows modern Greek; a Keeper may prefer 'pan-to-KRAH-tor'.

Editor: practice and carry no longer repeat day 1353's look-up-to-the-highest-point exercise; they now turn to the dome's point of everyone under one heaven. Framed the closing heaven line as the picture's, not the narrator's.
